1:
Henry organises the two verses as three privileges and calls them by their theological names. Election first: the Lord chose them not for merit nor for good works foreseen, and not because they were already a peculiar people, but that they might be so by his grace. Then adoption — Israel is called a son not because God needed children but because they were orphans and needed a father. Then sanctification, a people separated, devoted, governed by a holy law and graced by a holy tabernacle; and if they are holy, he adds, they are indebted to the grace that made them so. Gill divides the sonship differently and more cautiously: some were children by the special grace of adoption, all by national adoption, and it is the second that lays the nation under obligation. Ellicott makes the same fact structural rather than devotional, this sonship being the foundation of every law of ceremonial and moral holiness in the Pentateuch.

What the prohibition against cutting forbids is the one substantial division here, and Clarke stands alone. He takes it of the hair, since it was a custom among idolatrous nations to consecrate their hair to their deities, and mentions incisions in the flesh only as an occasional accompaniment. Henry takes it of the flesh throughout, and finds three things forbidden at once: cutting at funerals, whether to express grief or to appease the infernal deities with one's own blood; the self-wounding of idol worship, as with the prophets of Baal at 1 Kings 18:28; and marking the body for a particular deity, which he calls inexcusable in men who already bore the marks of the Lord in circumcision. Gill agrees the reference is to Gentile custom and extends it past mourning to their religious services generally. Ellicott adds that the precept is repeated with little variation from Leviticus 19:28, and corrects the second clause: the baldness is apparently on the forehead, though the word here is generally used of baldness at the back of the head.

Henry then draws two consequences, and Wesley states them in the same order and very nearly the same words — the parent's charge to little children playing with knives, and the design of crossing providences to remove what we might hurt ourselves with. Wesley is abridging Henry here rather than testifying independently, and the agreement should be discounted accordingly. The substance is that the body may not be deformed on any account, and that grief itself may not be exasperated past measure. On the second Henry quotes a Jewish writer at second hand: if a man's father dies he is not to cut himself, for he is not fatherless but has a Father who is great, living and permanent, whereas the man who has said to a stock, Thou art my father, has none to help him in time of need, and therefore weeps and cuts himself and makes himself bald.

On the second verse Ellicott is the only one to notice that it is repeated word for word from Deuteronomy 7:6 apart from an added conjunction, and that the same principle grounds two different things in the two places — there the destruction of the monuments of idolatry, here personal dignity and purity; he prefers peoples to nations, the contrast being between commonwealths and their institutions. At the third verse the question is why anything should be abominable at all. Gill answers that a thing is such either in its own nature or because God has forbidden it. Wesley reduces it to the second alone, unclean and forbidden by God and therefore to be abominable to us. Ellicott takes the same line, the distinctions being alike established and removed by the Creator, but allows what nobody else allows, that they had a sanitary purpose besides. Keil declines the question, referring the whole exposition of what follows to Leviticus 11.
4:
What this list is for, given that Leviticus 11 has already given one, is answered three ways. Ellicott states the structural difference exactly: Deuteronomy specifies the beasts that are to be eaten, Leviticus gives the exceptions, and the paragraph here answers to the earlier one point for point. Clarke had treated the subject at length in the earlier place and refers the reader back for the general question, but insists that particulars appear here which are not in Leviticus at all and must be handled where they stand. Keil takes the opposite course and declines the chapter, reporting that the laws are repeated in all essential points and sending the exposition away to Leviticus; his block then reproduces the bare biblical text and breaks off inside it.

Clarke's treatment is unlike anything else in the chapter. He classifies each animal by Linnaean order, genus and species — the ox as Bos, the sheep as Ovis, the goat as Capra, all of the fifth order Pecora — and notes that the Hebrew terms are generic, covering bull, cow, heifer and calf under the one word, on the idiom by which son of man means any man. He then gives a reason for the law that nobody else gives: these animals live on the best vegetables, and having several stomachs their food is well concocted, so that the chyle formed from it is the purest because it is well refined before entering the blood. The permitted flesh is wholesome, and that is why it is permitted. Ellicott notices something different about the first three names, that they stand first because they are the sacrificial animals, and that the second and third are literally a young one of the sheep or of the goats — which is why the passover victim might by the letter of the law be either lamb or kid.

The identifications divide them sharply. On the third name Gill derives it from a root of redness and suggests the red deer, adding that in Arabic the word is used of a two-horned woodland animal swifter than a hart, and asks whether it may be the elk. Clarke rejects the fallow deer outright and makes it the buffalo, on a root meaning to be troubled or disordered and on the testimony of travellers who describe the creature as sullen, malevolent and every way brutal — a beast, he notes, served daily at Solomon's table according to 1 Kings 4:23, and eaten there as commonly as the ox is in England. He adds that this animal is not named in the parallel chapter at all. Ellicott attaches the buffalo to a different word again, the pygarg, and gives the wild goat as the Steinbock. Clarke admits the last two are past recovery: both words occur nowhere else in Hebrew, and the Greek name for the second means white buttocks and elsewhere denotes an eagle, though here it plainly means a quadruped; for the first he can only report a traveller's timorous goat resembling both goat and stag, which is what the old versions called a goat-stag. Ellicott draws from the list a conclusion nobody else draws — if all these creatures were then to be found in Palestine, there must have been far more uncleared land than there has been for many centuries since. Gill, who has no interest in the natural history, reduces the whole to the two rules that decide the question, the parted hoof and the chewed cud, either alone being insufficient.
8: Gill is the only witness across these two verses, and he treats the rule of the waters as the exact counterpart of the rule of the beasts. There the test was double and both marks had to be present together; here it is double as well, fins and scales. The permission is put positively — these ye shall eat of all that are in the waters — and the prohibition follows as its converse, so that whatever wants either mark is unclean and may not be eaten. He allows no exceptions and no degrees. A creature is not made partly clean by carrying one of the two marks, any more than the camel was made clean by chewing the cud while failing to divide the hoof.
11:
The birds are handled by negation, and Gill reports the rabbinic explanation of why. Only the unclean sorts are named, so that everything left unnamed may be reckoned clean and fit for food; and the reason given for that arrangement is that the clean kinds are the more numerous, so it is the shorter list that gets written out. He supplies the positive marks as well, from the Targum: a clean bird is one that has a craw, whose crop is naked, that has a superfluous talon, and that is not rapacious. It is a test of habits and anatomy together, and unlike the double test for beasts and for fish it is nowhere stated in the verse itself.

All three who work on the names converge on a textual difficulty and describe it differently. Ellicott counts the list here against the earlier one and finds all the same birds with a single exception, then narrows the problem: where Leviticus has two names, this place has three, and the three are strikingly close to one another in form. Clarke locates the trouble in the translation rather than the text — the first of the two words in the earlier chapter is improperly rendered vulture there and really means a kite or glede, while the third name here is a different creature altogether and is properly rendered vulture. Gill puts it in terms of the letters: the extra name here differs from the one in the earlier list by a single character, the two characters are much alike and are sometimes exchanged, and the two names would then be one bird under two spellings — though he keeps open the alternative that a distinct sort is meant, perhaps the black vulture. He canvasses the Targums for the identifications, which give the vulture in one place and a white vulture in another, and adds from a Greek naturalist that there are two sorts, the one smaller and whiter, the other larger and of many colours. The name he is chiefly concerned with, he observes, takes its sense in the earlier chapter from flying and here from seeing, for which the bird is remarkable.
19:
On the winged creeping things and the clean fowls Gill is the only voice, and both his notes come from the Targum. The first paraphrase makes the unclean class concrete — flies, wasps or hornets, and the worms of lentils and of beans which separate from the food and fly like birds — so that the prohibition covers the insect at the stage when it takes wing. The second permits the locust by name, which he backs from another Jewish writer, so that the clean fowls of the verse are not limited to birds at all.

At the next verse Calvin carries almost the whole weight, and his first move is to define the case narrowly. The carcase meant is an animal dead of hunger or disease, which contracted its impurity from the manner of its death though in itself it was of a clean kind; flesh torn by beasts falls under the same rule, the deformity of the laceration being counted as uncleanness. The end of the precept, he says, is given in the reason subjoined to it — that they are a holy people — and it is that reason, not any property of the meat, that the law rests on. He then does something the text does not invite: he separates this prohibition from the prohibition of blood with which it is elsewhere conjoined, on the ground that the penalties differ, since the man who eats blood is cut off from the people while the man who eats carrion washes and is unclean until evening. Moses, he observes, does not always arrange his precepts in order but adduces promiscuously what belongs to different classes. His argument that the meat is really contaminated is drawn from the disposal: God would not command food intended for man to be thrown to dogs unless it carried a contagion that would pollute his holy ones.

The permission to give it to a stranger or sell it to an alien is where the difficulty lies, and Calvin states the objection against himself in the sharpest form — that this would be to supply the materials of sin, as one might hand a sword to a madman or pass stolen goods to another. His answer is that the Gentiles lay under no such distinction of meats in the first place, the prohibition being a mark of separation between them and the elect people rather than a judgement on the food; and he concedes that a harder question remains, since elsewhere stranger and home-born are bound alike. Ellicott reaches the same place from the grammar and reaches it more cleanly. The clause is literally and he will eat it, so what is indicated may be the common practice rather than the writer's intention; and the restrictions were meant to raise Israel above the common level, not to degrade the other nations by comparison — strangers were never compelled to eat what Israel refused, but left free to please themselves.

On the kid in its mother's milk the two who speak differ in scope. Ellicott notes only that this is the last of three appearances of the command, the other two both in Exodus. Clarke reports an opinion he does not endorse, that the precept concerns the paschal victim alone, which was not to be offered to God until it was weaned.
22:
All seven agree that this is not the tithe of Numbers 18, and they differ over almost everything else about it. Gill marks the distinction simply: the Levites' tithe was theirs to eat, this one the owners ate themselves, and the separating of it was therefore left to them. Henry does the arithmetic — the ground was tithed twice, so a fifth of the increase went to God and four parts in five remained for common use, which he calls an easy rent, the more so because God's part was spent to the payer's own benefit. Clarke lays out a whole cycle instead: the first tithe to the Levites, who paid a tenth of it to the priests; the second eaten by the owners in the first and second years, given to the Levites and the poor in the third, eaten by the owners again in the fourth and fifth, given to the poor in the sixth, and the seventh a sabbath when all things were common. Ellicott reports the Jewish consensus, that this tithe, the one at the end of the chapter and the one in Deuteronomy 26 are one and the same second tithe, and adds the distinction that matters: the first tithe was not accounted sacred, the second always was. Wesley identifies the second tithe with the third-year tithe outright, which the others keep apart.

Why the measuring was left to the owner is Henry's question. The law reposed a confidence in them and so tried their fear of God; God's part might be diminished by design or merely by oversight, and men who are stewards rather than owners of their estates must give a full account. He turns it into a rule of order — lay by first and lay out afterwards, since what has been set apart is easier to spend well and the proportion is more satisfying. Calvin notices that the law claims the tithe for God before saying who is to have it, and only later, when it commends the Levites, shows the use it is put to; from which he argues that to withhold the tithe is to defraud a brother of his maintenance, and to pay it grudgingly is unjust, the tribe having no inheritance in land and holding this by hereditary right.

At the next verse the single sanctuary raises a difficulty, and here Calvin breaks with everyone. He asks whether it can be consistent that all the tithes of the whole land should be carried to one place, and answers that as the Levites were dispersed through the country the command so read is absurd and would amount to destroying them by famine. He rejects the conjecture earlier commentators were driven to, that the people voluntarily set apart a further tithe for the journey, as an improbable doubling of the burden. His own reconstruction is that the Levites collected in their own neighbourhoods while a separate tithing went up to the sanctuary; distant tithes were set aside locally but accounted for at Jerusalem so that the distribution could be made even across families. Two supporting arguments are his own: that carrying grain up only for the Levites to carry it home again would be expense without advantage, and that the severe threats requiring the Levites to pay the priests faithfully would be pointless if the priests already held the whole quantity. Keil and Ellicott take the rule at face value and answer the practical problem instead — Keil by the permission to sell the tithe at home where the distance is too great and buy what the meal needs on arrival, Ellicott by noting that the arrangement differs in the third and sixth years, and that in the sabbatical year there was probably no tithe at all, there being no harvest and the profit of the earth being free to all.
24:
Whether the permission to turn the tithe into money is about the tithe at all is where Calvin parts from the rest, and his reasons are textual rather than theological. The ordinance for redeeming tithes by a money payment requires a fifth to be added, at Leviticus 27:31, and no fifth is mentioned here; and the explanation that follows speaks of bringing money instead of offerings and buying oxen, sheep, wine and strong drink with it. He concludes that the concession is for those whose distance made it burdensome to bring victims and gifts, who might buy at the sanctuary whatever they chose to offer, provided they offered nowhere else. Keil reads the same clause as plainly the tithe's commutation, and works on the wording: the Hebrew is give it up for silver, and the direction to bind the silver in the hand is a compressed expression for binding it in a purse and carrying it — the object being a joyful meal at the sanctuary to which the Levite was to be invited. Gill's note is the practical one, that money was the lighter carriage.

How far the buyer's liberty extends divides the next verse. Gill takes the clause at its widest: he might buy whatever provision he liked and found most agreeable to his appetite. Ellicott reports that the Jews were very particular in the opposite direction, permitting nothing to be bought that is not named here, and that the rules for it fill a treatise of the Talmud devoted to the second tithe. On the mention of strong drink the two who notice it draw different conclusions from the same word. Ellicott takes it to settle that its use is not sinful in itself, and observes that the Hebrew term passes into Greek in the first chapter of Luke 1:15. Clarke, having identified the drink elsewhere, treats the verse as evidence about the legislation as a whole, saying that this one verse is enough to show the Mosaic law made ample provision for the comfort and happiness of the people.

Keil alone looks ahead to the third year and states the rule that governs it: the whole tithe of that year's produce was to be brought out of the granary and left in the towns, to feed the Levite, the stranger, the widow and the orphan — not carried to the sanctuary at all, but followed by a confession made before the Lord. On the Levite of the present verse Gill is brief and exact: he was not to be forgotten in this any more than in the first tithe, and not to be left behind but taken along to share the meal.
28:
Whether the third year introduces a further tithe or redirects an existing one is the question the entry turns on. Gill reports the case for a third: one Jewish authority held it did not excuse the second, and one copy of a deuterocanonical book has its writer giving a third tithe to the repair of the temple, though another has him giving it to the stranger, the fatherless and the widow, which fits the verse better. Against that he sets the general Jewish view: after the first tithe is separated, another is taken from the remainder in the third and sixth years from the sabbatical and given to the poor, so that in those two years there is no second tithe but the poor's tithe instead. Ellicott records the same name for it and the same identification. Calvin is blunter than either: those who think another kind of tithe is meant are mistaken, and the passage is a correction or interpretation of the law, framed lest the priests and Levites alone should consume the whole and no part reach the poor.

Calvin then does the arithmetic that makes the rule work. The third year is not every third year running but counted from the sabbatical, since otherwise the reckoning would repeatedly fall on the year when the land rested and there was neither sowing nor reaping. Wesley settles a smaller ambiguity in the same clause, that at the end of three years means in the third year, as the parallel at Deuteronomy 26:12 states, and that the added words the same year are there to prevent anyone taking it of the fourth.

Why the ministry was left in this position draws two explanations that point in opposite directions. Clarke makes the dependence deliberate and forward-looking: much of the Levite's support hung on the freewill offerings of the people, and God chose to make his ministers thus dependent so that they might be moved to labour for the people's spiritual profit, and the people, blessed under that ministry, might feel it a duty and a privilege to maintain them. Calvin explains the same arrangement by what it takes away. The Levites having been well provided for through two years, it was equitable that they should admit their poor brethren to a share; something was withdrawn from their abundance lest they give themselves to luxurious habits, and by this means not more than a twelfth part was left them.

At the last verse the question is who takes what, and a rabbinic reading divides them. Ellicott reports the opinion that the Levite comes for the first tithe while the stranger, the fatherless and the widow take the second, and rejects it — there is no proof that anything but the second tithe is in view anywhere in the passage, and the Levite always shared with the poor. Gill follows the same authority further, allowing that the Levite did indeed take the first tithe but denying that it is what is meant here, and reporting that the poor were not bound to eat this at the sanctuary as they were bound to eat the second tithe of the two preceding years. Ellicott keeps the opinion for a different reason: modern critics urge that the tithe law here contradicts the law in Numbers 18, yet the Jews who kept the whole law saw no discrepancy and read this precept as implying that one — and a nation is unlikely to have consented to pay double tithes perpetually if the two laws had been at odds. The distinction he draws is that the first was an ordinary rate for the ministry with no sacredness attaching to it, while the second was taken for God, and was either a joyful family feast or a gift to his poor, a table spread by the God of Israel for his own guests.
